questions.prompt: Cinderline emails Halvern a weekly CSV of line 2 defects, and Halvern forwards it to an outside consultant. Which control can Cinderline still apply to the consultant's reading of that file?

options.text: None: once delivered, the copy is enforced only by whoever holds it and by the agreement.
options.rationale: A copy carries no link back to Cinderline's catalog or sharing server, so nothing technical still applies to it.

options.text: Revoking Halvern's recipient stops the consultant opening the file.
options.rationale: An emailed file involves no recipient object; revocation acts on share requests, not on delivered bytes.

options.text: Rotating the export's token expires the file.
options.rationale: An exported CSV has no token; tokens authorize share requests, not files already copied.

options.text: Removing Halvern from a Unity Catalog group blocks the file.
options.rationale: Unity Catalog governs reads through Cinderline's catalog; a file on someone's laptop is outside it.

questions.prompt: A teammate updates a notebook to the new naming by changing spark.read.format("deltaSharing") to format("openSharing"). What happens on the next run?

options.text: The read fails because no Spark data source is registered under the new name.
options.rationale: Documentation renames do not rename code; the connector's documented format name is deltaSharing.

options.text: It works, because OpenSharing is an alias the connector accepts.
options.rationale: The connector's documentation registers and uses only deltaSharing; nothing establishes an alias.

options.text: It works but reads through a slower compatibility path.
options.rationale: There is no compatibility path; an unregistered format name is simply not resolved.

options.text: It revokes the recipient's token until the name is fixed.
options.rationale: A client-side format string cannot change the provider's recipient or token state.

questions.prompt: The week after the engineer who created Halvern's share left Cinderline, Halvern can still list the share but reading the view returns a permission-denied status for that object. The recipient, token and grant are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The share's owner was the departed engineer, whose account no longer holds SELECT on the view.
options.rationale: The API reference requires the share owner to keep SELECT on every shared table; losing it makes the object report permission denied.

options.text: Halvern's bearer token expired.
options.rationale: An expired token fails every request, including listing the share, which still works here.

options.text: Halvern's IP address left the recipient's allowed list.
options.rationale: An IP restriction would also block the listing request that still succeeds.

options.text: History sharing was disabled on the view.
options.rationale: History sharing affects only reads of older versions or timestamps; a current read needs none.

questions.prompt: Halvern analyses in pandas notebooks, has no Databricks workspace, and has ruled out an identity-provider integration this quarter. What does Cinderline send first so Halvern can read the share?

options.text: An activation link from which Halvern downloads the credential file once.
options.rationale: Open sharing with token authentication starts with an activation link; the file carries the endpoint and bearer token.

options.text: Nothing: Halvern must first send Cinderline its sharing identifier.
options.rationale: A sharing identifier comes from a recipient's Unity Catalog metastore, which Halvern does not have.

options.text: A Unity Catalog grant to Halvern engineers' user accounts.
options.rationale: Halvern's people are not identities in Cinderline's metastore; sharing grants go to a recipient object.

options.text: An OIDC federation policy for Halvern's identity provider.
options.rationale: Federation needs an identity-provider integration, which Halvern has ruled out for now.

questions.prompt: Cinderline shares a whole defects table and plans to have Halvern's client send a predicate hint for line = 2 so Halvern sees only line 2. What does the protocol allow the server to return?

options.text: Files that also contain other lines, because hints are best effort; the restriction must be in the shared object.
options.rationale: The protocol calls hint filtering best effort and requires clients to filter; a view or partition specification is the boundary.

options.text: Exactly the line 2 rows, because the server must apply every hint.
options.rationale: The server may skip a hint it cannot evaluate and may return files that do not match.

options.text: An error, because recipients cannot send predicates.
options.rationale: Predicate hints are optional fields of the read request that recipients may send.

options.text: Only files already cached on Halvern's client.
options.rationale: Caching by file id is a client choice; it does not change what the server returns.

questions.prompt: Halvern reads the shared view at 09:05 (version 42) into a pandas DataFrame. Cinderline commits version 43 at 09:40. At 10:00 Halvern's analyst re-runs a chart built on the DataFrame without re-reading. Which statement is true?

options.text: The chart still shows version 42; only a new read of the share returns version 43.
options.rationale: The DataFrame is a copy made at 09:05; the protocol serves the latest version only to a new read.

options.text: The chart shows version 43, because shared data is live.
options.rationale: Live applies to each read through the protocol; a DataFrame already in memory is not re-read.

options.text: The chart fails because the table changed after it was read.
options.rationale: A local copy does not consult the provider when it is used, so nothing fails.

options.text: The chart shows version 43 only if history sharing is enabled.
options.rationale: History sharing serves older versions on request; it never refreshes a local copy.

questions.prompt: At 14:00 Cinderline removes Halvern's grant and rotates the token with zero seconds. At 14:02 Halvern reports that a file download completed; at 14:03 its new query fails. What does this evidence show?

options.text: Revocation worked: the download used a file URL issued before 14:00 that had not expired, and the next request was refused.
options.rationale: Issued URLs carry their own expiration timestamps, while every new request needs the revoked access.

options.text: Revocation failed: any transfer after 14:00 proves the token still works.
options.rationale: A pre-signed file URL does not present the bearer token; it is limited by its own expiry.

options.text: The rotation extended the old token's life to cover the download.
options.rationale: Rotation can only shorten the existing token's expiry, never extend it.

options.text: The 14:03 failure is a network fault unrelated to revocation.
options.rationale: A refused request right after revocation is the expected result; nothing points to a network fault.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's MES database administrator sees 3,000 queries last week from one database user, cl_federation, and asks which Cinderline analysts ran them. Where is that answer kept?

options.text: On Cinderline's Databricks side, in its query history and audit records, because the database only sees the connection's credential.
options.rationale: Unity Catalog checks each analyst's own privileges, so the platform knows who ran each query; the source sees one user.

options.text: In the MES database logs, which record each Databricks user's name.
options.rationale: With a stored-credential connection the source authenticates the connection's user for every query.

options.text: Nowhere: federated queries are not attributed to people.
options.rationale: Unity Catalog authorizes the analyst before the query runs, so the query is attributed on the Databricks side.

options.text: In the foreign catalog's comment field.
options.rationale: A comment is static descriptive metadata; it records nothing about queries.

questions.prompt: EXPLAIN FORMATTED for a federated query shows that the remote SQL sent to the MES database has no WHERE clause, although your query filters on plant_code_of(order_code), a Databricks function. What happens at run time?

options.text: The source returns every row for the selected columns, and Databricks applies the filter afterwards.
options.rationale: A predicate absent from the remote query is not evaluated at the source; it runs locally after transfer.

options.text: The source applies the filter anyway because Databricks sends it separately.
options.rationale: The remote query text is what the source runs; nothing else is sent for it to evaluate.

options.text: The query fails until the function is removed.
options.rationale: Predicates that cannot be pushed are evaluated in Databricks; the query still runs, only more slowly.

options.text: Only the first fetch batch is returned.
options.rationale: Fetch size sets rows per batch, not how many rows the query returns.

questions.prompt: Minutes after a Delta commit, an Iceberg engine counts 10,412 rows in a UniForm-enabled table while Delta readers count 10,530. What do you check first?

options.text: The converted_delta_version property on the Iceberg side against the latest Delta version.
options.rationale: Iceberg metadata is generated asynchronously after the commit; the property shows which Delta version Iceberg readers see.

options.text: Whether VACUUM removed files the Iceberg engine needs.
options.rationale: Missing files would cause read errors, not a consistent count from an older snapshot.

options.text: Whether column mapping was switched off.
options.rationale: Column mapping cannot be turned off once enabled, and it does not change row counts.

options.text: Whether the table has too many partitions.
options.rationale: Partitioning affects layout and pruning, not which snapshot a reader sees.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's reliability team runs open-source Spark with an Iceberg REST client against Unity Catalog. Its service principal owns the schema and holds ALL PRIVILEGES on it, and the metastore admin has enabled external access. Loading a table still fails with a permission error. What is missing?

options.text: EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA on the schema, granted explicitly by the catalog owner.
options.rationale: The API reference says it is excluded from schema ownership and ALL PRIVILEGES and must be granted explicitly.

options.text: SELECT on the table.
options.rationale: ALL PRIVILEGES on the schema already covers reading its tables; the missing piece is specific to outside engines.

options.text: A recipient token for the team.
options.rationale: Recipient tokens belong to sharing with other organizations; an internal engine uses the catalog's own interface.

options.text: UniForm enabled for the whole metastore.
options.rationale: UniForm is a per-table setting and grants nobody credentials.

selfQuestions.prompt: Halvern wants an unattended nightly Python job to read the share. Propose a credential policy (expiry, rotation, network restriction, where the file lives) and say what you do if the file is emailed to the wrong person.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Create the recipient with a token expiry set by Cinderline's policy (for example 90 days, a synthetic value) and an IP access list naming the CIDR range the job leaves from. Halvern keeps the profile file in its secret manager, not on a shared drive, and the job reads it from there. Rotate a few days before expiry with a short overlap, sending the new activation link only to the named contact. If the file is mis-sent, rotate with zero seconds so the old token stops at once, confirm the new file reached only the named contact, and review provider-side access records for reads since the mis-send. When Halvern's identity provider can be integrated, move to OIDC federation so no long-lived secret exists.
selfQuestions.reasoning: A bearer token works for whoever holds it, so the policy limits its lifetime, where it can be used from and who holds it; a zero-second rotation is the documented immediate cut. OIDC federation or a shorter expiry are acceptable alternatives.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline's reliability team wants Halvern's coating batch parameters in its daily scrap dashboard, refreshed each morning and kept three years for audits. Halvern now also offers federated read access to a replica of its batch database. Decide between ingestion and access-in-place, and justify the choice with freshness, source load, history and failure behaviour.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Ingest. The dashboard reads the parameters hundreds of times a day, so a daily copy into a governed Delta table loads Halvern's replica once per day instead of once per dashboard refresh. The three-year audit needs reproducible history the source may not keep, and Delta versions give it. A source outage delays one load and leaves yesterday's copy answering, instead of breaking every dashboard view. Freshness of last night meets the stated need. Keep federated access for an engineer's occasional question about today's batch, and record the copy's owner, retention and deletion rule.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Query frequency, the audit's need for history and the source's load tolerance all favour a copy, while the freshness requirement does not demand live reads. A hybrid, with federation for occasional current questions, is an acceptable addition.

selfQuestions.prompt: Design the output of a clean room notebook that correlates Cinderline's warranty returns with a supplier's compound batches so that neither side learns the other's row-level records. What does the output contain, and what do reviewers on both sides check before approving?
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The output is one table of counts and return rates per compound batch and month, with batch and month as the only keys, written only for groups above an agreed minimum size (for example at least 20 returns, a synthetic threshold) and with no customer, part serial or inspection identifiers. Reviewers check that every write targets the output catalog, that joins are aggregated before writing, that the suppression rule is applied before the write rather than after, that no debug cell prints rows, and that the runner list names only the intended collaborators. Any later change to the notebook goes back through review.
selfQuestions.reasoning: What leaves a clean room is exactly what the approved notebook writes, so the output schema and the review are the real controls, not the room itself. Stricter thresholds or noise-adding methods are acceptable alternatives when groups are small.

selfQuestions.prompt: Halvern's engineer now reports that their notebook environment cannot read the share after all. Using the six questions, what changes in Cinderline's decision, and what exactly do you tell the security lead?
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: First check whether any client Halvern can run reads the protocol, such as the pandas connector in another environment, because that would keep the governed share. If none can, fall back to a weekly extract of the same view with written retention and deletion terms. The six answers change: the rows move into Halvern's storage, enforcement ends at delivery, cost becomes export effort plus Halvern's storage, revocation becomes impossible, freshness becomes weekly, and failure becomes silent, so add a check that each export arrived. Tell the security lead plainly that access can no longer be withdrawn, only governed by the agreement, and ask for explicit acceptance.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The fallback follows the field guide's rule that an unrevocable copy must be accepted knowingly; re-answering all six questions shows every consequence, not only the obvious one. Delaying the collaboration until a supported client exists is an acceptable alternative.

beats.title: Copy, share and federate move different things to different places
beats.outcome: Place copy, governed share and federation on one diagram of data movement, enforcement and ownership.
beats.explanation: Cinderline can meet Halvern's request three ways. A copy writes filtered rows into Halvern's systems, and from then on only Halvern's controls apply. A [[dbxfe-sharing-pattern-concept|governed share]] leaves the rows in Cinderline's storage and checks the recipient on every read. Federation runs a query against the other party's database, which checks the connection's credential. Notice in each state where the rows land and where the enforcement node sits, and which state has no enforcement at all.

samajh.text: Socho Cinderline ke paas ek zaroori file hai jo supplier ko chahiye. Pehla tareeka: photocopy bhej do — ab woh copy supplier ki almari mein hai, aap usse wapas nahi le sakte. Doosra: supplier aapke office ke reading room mein aake padhe — entry aapka guard har baar check karta hai, aur kal se entry band bhi kar sakte ho. Teesra: aap supplier ko phone karke unki file se jawab maango — jawab dena ya na dena unke haath mein hai.
samajh.mapping: The photocopy is a copy, the reading room with its guard is a governed share whose sharing server checks each visit, and the phone call is federation answered under the source's own credential check.
samajh.boundary: Unlike a reading room, a share's reader carries what it read into its own tools, and a federated answer lands in your compute, so saved results become copies anyway.

handbook.markdown:
The field guide's six questions give every pattern the same interview. Asked of Cinderline's options for Halvern:

| Question | Copy | Governed share | Federation |
|---|---|---|---|
| What moves | Filtered rows, into Halvern's storage | Files per read, from Cinderline's storage to Halvern's client | Rows per query, from the source into the querier's compute |
| Who enforces | Whoever holds the file | The sharing server, per request | Unity Catalog for people, the source for the connection's credential |
| Who pays in kind | Analyst time; Halvern's storage | Cinderline's storage and transfer; Halvern's compute | The source's load; the querier's compute |
| Revocation | None | Stops future reads | The source disables the credential |
| Freshness | As of the export | Current at each read | Live at each query |
| Failure | A silent gap when an export is missed | A visible read error | A failed query; a slowed source |

Two refinements matter. First, a governed share is access-in-place only until the recipient saves a result: from then on that result is a copy in the recipient's systems, and the copy column applies to it. Second, direction matters: federation is how Cinderline reads a partner's system, whereas a share is how Cinderline lets a partner read Cinderline's. A partnership with two directions usually needs two answers.

A clean room is the fourth answer when neither party may see the other's rows; it moves computation to both datasets and releases only outputs. It comes later because it needs both parties on Unity Catalog and is not available everywhere. Inspect three things before choosing: who must be able to withdraw access, whether the other side's tooling can read a share, and whether the source's owner accepts query load.

beats.recap: A copy moves rows and ends control; a share checks each read; federation queries the source in place.

beats.title: OpenSharing names the product; the protocol keeps its identifiers
beats.outcome: Separate current product names from protocol identifiers that code must keep unchanged.
beats.explanation: Databricks' current documentation calls its sharing product family [[dbxfe-sharing-opensharing-concept|OpenSharing]]; the historical delta-sharing documentation URL now leads to the OpenSharing overview. The open protocol specification is still titled Delta Sharing Protocol, and code keeps its spellings: the Spark format deltaSharing, the delta_sharing Python package, profile fields such as shareCredentialsVersion, and the API resources shares, recipients and providers. Notice in the table which column you may rename in prose, and in the second state what a mechanical rename does to running code.

handbook.markdown:
Databricks renamed the documentation for its sharing product family: the page now titled "What is OpenSharing?" is where the historical delta-sharing URL leads, according to this repository's reviewed source record. Names at other layers did not move, and several are identifiers that code resolves exactly.

```python
import delta_sharing  # package name unchanged

profile = "/secrets/halvern/cinderline.share"  # synthetic path
table_url = profile + "#halvern_line2_quality.share.line2_coated_defects_by_batch"
pdf = delta_sharing.load_as_pandas(table_url)

sdf = spark.read.format("deltaSharing").load(table_url)  # Spark connector format name
```

The profile file's fields (`shareCredentialsVersion`, `endpoint`, `bearerToken`, `expirationTime`), the protocol's REST routes, the Databricks API resources (`shares`, `recipients`, `providers`, `recipient_activation`) and the API's own wording, which still describes a "delta sharing authentication type", all keep their spelling. The protocol specification read for this module is titled Delta Sharing Protocol.

How to write about it: use OpenSharing for the Databricks product and its documentation, Delta Sharing for the open protocol and its clients, and quote identifiers verbatim in code font. When searching older material, search both names; a concept with Delta Sharing as an alias keeps the old term findable.

What fails if you get it wrong: a renamed format string produces a data-source-not-found error in Spark; a renamed import fails in Python; a profile with renamed fields is no longer the format the client parses. None of these is a permission problem, so do not start the diagnosis at the recipient or the grant.

beats.recap: Say OpenSharing in prose; keep deltaSharing, delta_sharing and the API resource names in code.

beats.title: A share lists objects; a grant decides which recipient reads them
beats.outcome: Set up a share, a recipient and a grant, and diagnose a failure caused by the share owner's privileges.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-sharing-share-concept|share]] is a container in Cinderline's metastore listing existing objects, here one view of line 2 coated-part defects. A [[dbxfe-sharing-recipient-concept|recipient]] represents Halvern, and a grant of SELECT on the share connects them. The API reference adds a dependency: the share owner must keep SELECT on every shared table, so a group should own the share. Notice in the second state that listing still works while the view reads as permission denied.
beats.hint: Listing works, so the token and network are fine; look at what the object itself depends on.
beats.recap: Grant SELECT on the share to the recipient, and let a group own the share so reads survive staff changes.

beats.title: The recipient's platform decides how the recipient proves who it is
beats.outcome: Choose Databricks-to-Databricks or open sharing from the recipient's platform and name what each exchanges.
beats.explanation: How a recipient proves its identity depends on its platform. A supplier with a Unity Catalog workspace sends its sharing identifier, cloud:region:metastore-uuid; no token exists, and its admin creates a catalog from the share ([[dbxfe-sharing-d2d-concept|Databricks-to-Databricks sharing]]). Any other supplier gets [[dbxfe-sharing-open-concept|open sharing]]: an activation link that downloads a credential file once, or OIDC federation with short-lived tokens from its identity provider. Notice which side holds a secret in each state.

handbook.markdown:
The Databricks API reference describes two sharing modes and chooses between them by one fact: does the recipient have access to a Unity Catalog-enabled Databricks workspace?

**Databricks-to-Databricks sharing.** The recipient's metastore admin sends its sharing identifier, `cloud:region:metastore-uuid`. Cinderline creates the recipient with it (authentication type `DATABRICKS`); in SQL, as previously read, `CREATE RECIPIENT pellmark_polymers USING ID 'aws:eu-west-1:...';`. On the recipient's side the share appears under a provider object, and the admin creates a catalog from it (the API's Delta Sharing catalog, built from a provider name and a share name), for example `CREATE CATALOG cinderline_seals USING SHARE cinderline.pellmark_seals;`, then grants `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `SELECT` to its own users. Cinderline never sees the recipient's people; the recipient's grants decide who reads.

**Open sharing.** For a recipient on any other platform, Cinderline creates a recipient with authentication type `TOKEN`. Databricks generates an activation link, and the recipient downloads a credential file from it once; the API reference tells recipients to treat that file as a secret and not to share it outside their organization. The alternative is `OIDC_FEDERATION`: a federation policy on the recipient validates short-lived tokens from the recipient's own identity provider, for a person reading through a BI tool or a machine running a nightly job.

What to decide: the mode follows the recipient's platform, not preference. Then decide who at the recipient owns the credential or the catalog, and how Cinderline will learn when that person leaves. The reverse direction also exists: a Databricks workspace can register a non-Databricks sharing server as a provider by supplying that server's profile.

beats.recap: A Unity Catalog recipient sends an identifier and uses no token; anyone else gets a one-time credential file or OIDC federation.

beats.title: A bearer token works for whoever holds it until it expires
beats.outcome: Design a recipient credential policy with expiry, network restriction, rotation and an emergency cut.
beats.explanation: The [[dbxfe-sharing-credential-concept|credential file]] holds shareCredentialsVersion, the server endpoint, a bearer token and an optional expirationTime; the protocol treats a missing expiry as never expiring. Whoever holds the file can read, so Cinderline sets an expiry, restricts source addresses with an IP access list, and rotates. Rotation issues a new token and can only shorten the old one's life; zero seconds ends it at once. Notice the one-day overlap at day 80 and the immediate cut on day 95.

handbook.markdown:
The credential file is JSON in the protocol's profile format (synthetic values):

```json
{
  "shareCredentialsVersion": 1,
  "endpoint": "https://sharing.example.invalid/delta-sharing/",
  "bearerToken": "redacted-synthetic-token",
  "expirationTime": "2026-12-22T00:00:00.0Z"
}
```

The protocol makes `expirationTime` optional and says that without it the token can be seen as never expiring. On the Databricks side a recipient's token carries an expiration time, the recipient can carry an IP access list of CIDR ranges, and the owner can rotate:

```python
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from databricks.sdk.service.sharing import IpAccessList

w = WorkspaceClient()
w.recipients.update(name="halvern_coatings",
    ip_access_list=IpAccessList(allowed_ip_addresses=["203.0.113.0/24"]))  # synthetic range
w.recipients.rotate_token(name="halvern_coatings",
    existing_token_expire_in_seconds=86400)  # old token ends in one day
```

`rotate_token` issues a new token and sets the existing token's expiry; the API reference says it can only move that expiry earlier, never later, and 0 expires it immediately. The new activation link goes to the named contact; the old file stops working when its token expires.

A policy that holds up: an expiry that forces rotation a few times a year (the length is Cinderline's policy, not a product default); an IP list matching the recipient's job egress; the file in the recipient's secret store rather than a shared drive; a rotation calendar with a short overlap; a zero-second rotation for any leak. Where the recipient has an identity provider, OIDC federation removes the file altogether. What to inspect: the recipient's token list and expiry, its activation state (the API reports an empty activation URL once it has been used) and its IP list.

beats.recap: Give every token an expiry, an IP list and a rotation plan; zero-second rotation is the emergency cut.

beats.title: The sharing server authorizes; the Parquet bytes come from Cinderline's storage
beats.outcome: Trace a shared-table read from bearer token to direct file download and name its security and cost consequences.
beats.explanation: Halvern's client sends a read request with its bearer token. The sharing server checks the recipient's grant, then answers with the table's Parquet files as [[dbxfe-sharing-presigned-concept|short-lived HTTPS URLs]], each with its own expiry, or with temporary storage credentials. The client downloads from Cinderline's storage and filters locally, because predicate hints are best effort. Notice in the third state that the server is no longer in the data path, and that the hint cannot act as a boundary.
beats.hint: Separate who checks the request from where the bytes travel.

handbook.markdown:
The protocol request that returns data is "Read Data from a Table", a POST authorized by the bearer token. Its optional body fields shape the answer without being guarantees:

- `predicateHints` and `jsonPredicateHints`: filters the server may use to skip files; best effort, and the server may return files that do not match.
- `limitHint`: a row budget the server may use with file statistics; also best effort. The client must still apply its own filter and limit.
- `version` or `timestamp`: an older snapshot, served only when history sharing is enabled for that table.

The answer is a stream of JSON lines: protocol and metadata, then one `file` entry per data file with a `url`, an `id`, the partition values, the size, optional statistics and an optional `expirationTimestamp`. The client downloads each URL directly from the provider's cloud storage. A server may instead offer directory-based access: temporary read-only cloud credentials for the table's root, also with an expiration time, for engines that read the Delta log themselves.

Three consequences follow. Security: the restriction must be in the shared object (a view, a purpose-built table or a partition specification), because a hint is not a boundary. Cost: the bytes leave Cinderline's storage, so cross-region or cross-cloud reads create transfer on the storage owner's bill; check current cloud pricing before sharing a large table far away. Compatibility: the protocol's delta response format is what enables reading tables with advanced reader features such as deletion vectors or column mapping, and a client that did not request that format must fail if the server answers in it, so test the recipient's client version before changing the table's features.

beats.recap: The server authorizes and lists files; the bytes come straight from the provider's storage; hints are not boundaries.

beats.title: A share reads the current version; a copy starts going stale when it lands
beats.outcome: Distinguish a fresh read, a stale saved copy and an opt-in historical read.
beats.explanation: Each read of a shared table returns its latest version, so a query is fresh when it runs. What Halvern saves is a copy, and it goes stale as soon as Cinderline commits again; the protocol's table-version call lets a client detect that. Older versions are served only when [[dbxfe-sharing-history-concept|history sharing]] is enabled, which is off by default. Notice in the second state that the DataFrame stays at version 42 while a new read returns 43, a gap in [[dbxfe-sharing-freshness-concept|freshness]].

handbook.markdown:
Three freshness statements get confused.

1. A protocol read is fresh when it runs. Without `version` or `timestamp`, the server returns files for the latest table version, so two reads a minute apart can see different versions.
2. A saved result is a copy. A pandas DataFrame, an extract or a dashboard cache made from a read ages from the moment it is written. The protocol's Query Table Version call exists for this: a client that caches data can store the version it read and cheaply check whether the table has moved on.
3. History is opt-in. Reading an older version or timestamp is served only when history sharing is enabled on that object, and the Databricks API leaves `history_data_sharing_status` disabled unless it is set. A `start_version` on the shared object sets the lowest version recipients may query; without it they start from the version current when the object was added.

For incremental consumers the change data feed is a fourth option (see the extension card): the recipient reads changes between versions instead of re-reading the table.

In Halvern's timeline (synthetic): version 42 committed at 09:00 and read at 09:05 into a DataFrame; version 43 committed at 09:40. At 10:00 the DataFrame still holds version 42; only a new read returns 43. A Monday CSV export is four days behind by Friday, and nothing tells its reader so.

For federation the statement is simpler and harsher: each query reads the source as it is at that moment, and Databricks keeps no versions of it. For UniForm, the Iceberg view can trail the Delta view. When writing an agreement, say which of these you promise: fresh per read, fresh as of a stated schedule, or reproducible as of a version.

beats.recap: Reads are fresh, saved results go stale, and history is served only when enabled.

beats.title: Revocation stops the next request, not the bytes already delivered
beats.outcome: Draw the revocation timeline and plan a rehearsal that measures its tail.
beats.explanation: Cinderline can [[dbxfe-sharing-revocation-concept|revoke]] by removing Halvern's SELECT on the share, deleting the recipient, or rotating its token with zero seconds. The next request then fails. File URLs issued minutes earlier carry their own expiry, so a download already under way can finish, and whatever Halvern saved stays saved. Notice where the timeline passes out of Cinderline's control: the tail between revocation and the last URL expiry, and the copies that no revocation reaches.

samajh.text: Library membership cancel karo toh naya book issue nahi hota — kal counter pe jaoge toh mana ho jayega. Lekin jo book aaj subah issue hui thi woh due date tak aapke ghar pe hai, aur usme se jo notes aapne apni copy mein likh liye, woh hamesha aapke paas rahenge. Membership band karna aage ka rasta band karta hai, pichhla sab wapas nahi laata.
samajh.mapping: Cancelling the membership is removing the grant or rotating the token, the book already issued is a file URL still before its expiry, and the notes are the extracts the recipient saved.
samajh.boundary: A library expects the book back; a sharing provider gets nothing back, and the URL simply stops working at its expiry, so retention must be agreed in writing.

handbook.markdown:
Revocation levers on the provider side, in SQL as previously read and in the API reference:

```sql
REVOKE SELECT ON SHARE halvern_line2_quality FROM RECIPIENT halvern_coatings;  -- this share only
DROP RECIPIENT halvern_coatings;                                               -- every share
```

```python
w.recipients.rotate_token(name="halvern_coatings", existing_token_expire_in_seconds=0)
```

Removing a recipient's grant needs the share permissions (`USE_SHARE` and `SET_SHARE_PERMISSION`, or share ownership) but, unlike a new grant, not ownership of the recipient; deleting a recipient needs its ownership; zero-second rotation ends the current token at once. For a Databricks-to-Databricks recipient the grant removal is the lever, and the recipient's catalog stops returning data on its next query.

What revocation cannot reach follows from the read path. File URLs issued before revocation carry their own expiration timestamps, and nothing in the protocol recalls a URL already handed out; directory credentials likewise run to their expiry. Data the recipient saved lives in its systems. Revocation is therefore a statement about future requests, and the agreement has to cover retention and deletion of what was received.

The rehearsal, consistent with the field guide: before the first real read, grant the recipient a share of synthetic rows; have the recipient read from its own tooling; revoke; ask the recipient to read again and report the exact error; record the time from revocation to the first refused request and to the last successful file download. Keep that record with the decision, and repeat it after any change of recipient mode or tooling.

Afterwards inspect the share's grants (`SHOW GRANTS ON SHARE`), the recipient's token list, and the provider-side access records your platform keeps, confirming that the rehearsal's refused read appears there.

beats.recap: Revocation stops the next request; issued URLs run to expiry and saved copies stay.

beats.title: Federation queries the other system where it lives
beats.outcome: Explain the connection, the foreign catalog and the two authorization checks on a federated query.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-sharing-federation-concept|Lakehouse Federation]] registers a connection in Unity Catalog holding the source's host and credential options, then a [[dbxfe-sharing-foreign-concept|foreign catalog]] mirroring one database through it. A query passes two checks: Unity Catalog grants for the analyst, then the source's own authorization of the connection's credential. Rows travel per query and nothing is stored unless you write it; the overview describes the paths as read-only. Notice in the second state which identity the source database actually sees.
beats.recap: A foreign catalog passes Unity Catalog grants for people and the source's check of one connection credential.

beats.title: Pushdown decides how many rows cross the network
beats.outcome: Use EXPLAIN FORMATTED to predict how many rows a federated query moves.
beats.explanation: When a federated query runs, the connector translates what it can (filters, projections, limits) into the SQL sent to the source. A pushed predicate runs in the source; one it cannot translate runs in Databricks after every row has arrived. In this synthetic MES table the pushed date filter moves 1,840 rows, while a filter on a Databricks function moves 2.4 million. Notice that [[dbxfe-sharing-pushdown-concept|pushdown]] is read from the remote query in EXPLAIN FORMATTED, not assumed.
beats.hint: Look for the WHERE clause in the remote query text, not in your own SQL.

handbook.markdown:
The performance recommendations page, as reviewed in this repository, makes three points that decide a federated query's cost.

1. Some predicates push down and some stay local; which ones depends on the connector and the expression. A plain comparison on a column is the kind a connector can translate; a function the source does not know is not.
2. `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` exposes the remote query that will be sent, with a caveat that adaptive execution can change the plan at run time. That text is the evidence.
3. JDBC `fetchSize` controls how many rows arrive per batch, not how many connections read in parallel.

Synthetic example against Cinderline's MES database (`plant_code_of` is a fictional Databricks SQL function):

```sql
EXPLAIN FORMATTED
SELECT order_id, plant, qty
FROM mes.public.work_orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE'2026-09-01';     -- expect the WHERE clause in the remote query

EXPLAIN FORMATTED
SELECT order_id, plant, qty
FROM mes.public.work_orders
WHERE plant_code_of(order_code) = 'P2';   -- expect no WHERE clause remotely
```

In the first plan the remote query carries the date filter and about 1,840 rows cross the network; in the second the remote query selects every row (2.4 million in this synthetic table) and Databricks filters them. The fix is to express the predicate in columns the source understands, or to precompute the value at the source, not to raise the fetch size.

Troubleshooting order for a slow federated query: read the remote query; compare the rows the source returns with the rows the query keeps; check the source's own execution plan and load; only then consider batch settings. If the same heavy query runs every day, the question has changed from access to ingestion.

beats.recap: Read the remote query to know what the source filtered; everything else crossed the network.

beats.title: Ingest what you query often; access in place what you need now
beats.outcome: Choose between ingestion and access-in-place from freshness, frequency, history and source load.
beats.explanation: Ingestion copies source rows into governed Delta tables on a schedule or from change capture: repeated queries are fast, history is kept and the source is read once per run, but freshness is the last successful run and the copy must be owned and deleted. [[dbxfe-sharing-access-in-place-concept|Access-in-place]] through federation or a share reads the current state at query time, loads the source every time, and fails with it. Notice how the decision flips with query frequency and the need for history.

handbook.markdown:
Ingestion and access-in-place answer different questions. Ingestion (a Lakeflow Connect connector, a scheduled job or a pipeline) copies source data into governed Delta tables; the Lakeflow Connect overview groups its connectors into change-data-capture database ingestion, files, streaming and query-based ingestion, each with its own service model and source support. Access-in-place (federation for a system Cinderline queries, a share for data another party reads) leaves the data where it is and reads it at query time.

| Dimension | Ingest | Access in place |
|---|---|---|
| Freshness | As of the last successful run | Current at query time |
| Repeated queries | Fast, on Delta tables | Pay source latency each time |
| Source load | Once per run; change capture reads only changes | Every query |
| History | Delta versions you control | Only what the source keeps |
| Source outage | Last good copy still answers | Queries fail |
| Obligations | Own, retain and delete the copy | Keep the connection or share working |

The guidance that follows: ingest what dashboards and models read every day, what an audit must reproduce, and what a fragile or partner-owned source cannot serve repeatedly. Use access-in-place for occasional questions about the current state, for exploring a source before building a pipeline, and during a migration while the old system is still primary.

Two traps. A materialized result of a federated query is a copy again: it needs an owner, a refresh schedule and a retention rule. And an ingested copy of a partner's data is outside the partner's revocation: if the partner may need to withdraw it, write the retention and deletion terms before the first load. The ingestion module covers what an ingested copy needs next: keys, ordering and replay.

beats.recap: Ingest what is queried often or must be kept; access in place what is occasional and must be current.

beats.title: UniForm writes Iceberg metadata over the same Parquet files
beats.outcome: Explain how UniForm serves Iceberg readers from the same files, and its lag and limits.
beats.explanation: Delta Lake, Iceberg and Hudi tables are all Parquet files plus metadata. With [[dbxfe-sharing-uniform-concept|UniForm]] enabled, a Delta commit completes as usual, then Iceberg metadata for the same files is generated asynchronously, so one copy of the data serves both kinds of reader. The Iceberg view can lag, and frequent commits may be bundled. Notice in the first state that the Iceberg snapshot still reflects version 11, recorded in converted_delta_version, and in the second that an Iceberg writer stays excluded.

samajh.text: Ek hi kitaab mein do index hain — ek English mein, ek Hindi mein. Pages wahi hain, bas dhoondhne ka tareeka alag. Naya chapter judta hai toh English index usi waqt update hota hai, Hindi index thodi der baad banta hai. Tab tak Hindi index se dhoondhne wale ko naya chapter milta hi nahi. Aur agar koi Hindi index ke bharose pages jod ya phaad de, toh poori kitaab bigad sakti hai.
samajh.mapping: The pages are the shared Parquet files, the English index is the Delta log, and the Hindi index is the Iceberg metadata generated after each commit.
samajh.boundary: The lag is measurable through converted_delta_version, and the rule is stricter than in a library: Iceberg clients must never write, because the Delta log cannot see their changes.

handbook.markdown:
UniForm is a Delta Lake table setting, documented in the Delta Lake project's UniForm page (open source, read for this module) and by Databricks for Unity Catalog tables (confirm the current Databricks page and runtime before enabling):

```sql
ALTER TABLE quality.gold.defects SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.enableIcebergCompatV2' = 'true',
  'delta.universalFormat.enabledFormats' = 'iceberg');
```

What it does: after each Delta commit, the same compute generates Iceberg metadata that points at the same Parquet files, so one copy of the data serves both. Frequent commits may be bundled into one Iceberg commit, and while one generation is running a further commit does not start another. Iceberg metadata records `converted_delta_version` and `converted_delta_timestamp`; Delta and Iceberg version numbers do not align, so compare through those properties.

What it requires and changes: the Iceberg compatibility table feature requires column mapping (name or id mode) and upgrades the table's reader and writer protocol; column mapping cannot be turned off and the protocol upgrade cannot be undone, so every existing reader and writer must support them. The open-source documentation says UniForm does not work with deletion vectors enabled (a REORG upgrade purges them) and does not support the VOID type. Change Data Feed and Delta Sharing are Delta features with no Iceberg equivalent.

The limit that matters most: Iceberg clients may only read. The open-source page warns that an external Iceberg writer could perform cleanup Delta does not know about and destroy the table, so keep write access for Iceberg engines out of the design.

A sharing interaction worth knowing: column mapping raises the table's reader version, and the sharing protocol reads such tables through its delta response format, so an open-sharing recipient whose client cannot request that format may fail on the table once UniForm is enabled. Test the recipient's client first.

beats.recap: UniForm adds Iceberg metadata to the same files, a version or two behind, and Iceberg clients only read.

beats.title: An outside engine reads through a catalog that vends short-lived credentials
beats.outcome: Explain how an outside engine is authorized through a catalog and what Unity Catalog requires first.
beats.explanation: An engine outside Databricks finds tables through a catalog. With the [[dbxfe-sharing-iceberg-concept|Iceberg REST catalog]] protocol it asks for configuration, loads a table and may request [[dbxfe-sharing-vending-concept|vended credentials]]: short-lived storage access for that table. Unity Catalog vends them only after a metastore admin enables external access, off by default, and the catalog owner grants EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, which schema ownership and ALL PRIVILEGES do not include. Notice what the first state denies.
beats.hint: There are two switches: one on the metastore, one on the schema.

handbook.markdown:
Catalog interoperability has two directions.

**Outside engines reading Cinderline's tables.** The Apache Iceberg REST catalog API defines the conversation: the client calls `/v1/config` for defaults and overrides; it loads a table and receives the metadata location, the metadata and table-specific configuration; if it sent `X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation: vended-credentials`, the catalog may return short-lived storage credentials in the response. The open-source Unity Catalog project states compatibility with the Iceberg REST catalog API and the Hive metastore API. For the Databricks-managed Unity Catalog, the API reference for temporary table credentials states the governance: a metastore admin must enable external access (off by default), and the catalog owner must grant `EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA` explicitly, because it is excluded from schema ownership and `ALL PRIVILEGES`. The credentials are downscoped and short-lived: STS on AWS, a SAS on Azure, OAuth on Google Cloud.

```sql
-- SQL names a service principal by its application ID, not its display name.
GRANT EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA quality.gold TO `<svc-reliability-spark-application-id>`;  -- as previously read; confirm syntax
```

The Databricks endpoint for Iceberg REST clients is on the current Databricks page; this module does not assert its path.

**Unity Catalog reading other catalogs.** Catalog federation registers an external catalog such as a Hive metastore or AWS Glue through a connection; its tables appear in a foreign catalog and are read from object storage with Databricks compute.

Why this matters for governance: the catalog is the enforcement point. An engine handed raw bucket credentials bypasses every grant, row filter and audit the catalog would apply; vended credentials keep the catalog in the path and expire. When an external read fails, inspect in order: the metastore's external access setting, the `EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA` grant, the principal's table privileges, then the engine's catalog configuration.

beats.recap: Outside engines read through the catalog's vended credentials only after external access and EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA.

beats.title: A clean room shares computation and outputs, not rows
beats.outcome: Decide when a clean room fits and design its outputs so no row-level record leaves.
beats.explanation: When neither party may see the other's rows, a [[dbxfe-sharing-cleanroom-concept|clean room]] shares computation instead. Built on the sharing layer and serverless compute, it lets each collaborator add tables, views or volumes; notebooks are reviewed and run only by named collaborators, and results land in an output catalog. What leaves is whatever the approved notebook writes. Every collaborator is identified by a Unity Catalog metastore, so both need one. Notice which boxes each side can open, and which output would leak.

samajh.text: Do padosi check karna chahte hain ki kiska bijli ka bill season ke hisaab se zyada badha, par ek doosre ko apna bill dikhana nahi chahte. Dono apne bills ek bharosemand CA ko de dete hain. CA wahi hisaab lagata hai jispe dono ne pehle haan bola tha, aur sirf ek summary sheet deta hai. Bills CA ke office se bahar nahi jaate — bahar sirf summary aati hai.
samajh.mapping: Each neighbour's bill is a collaborator's table, the CA's office is the clean room's serverless environment, the agreed calculation is the reviewed notebook, and the summary sheet is the output catalog.
samajh.boundary: A CA applies judgement, but a clean room runs exactly the approved code: if that code writes raw rows to the output they leave, so reviewing the outputs is the real control.

handbook.markdown:
The Databricks API reference is the verified source here: "A clean room uses Delta Sharing and serverless compute to provide a secure and privacy-protecting environment where multiple parties can work together on sensitive enterprise data without direct access to each other's data." Its objects show how the boundary works.

- Collaborators are identified by a Unity Catalog global metastore identifier and an alias, so each party needs a Unity Catalog metastore. A central clean room has a cloud and a region, and can carry an egress network policy.
- Assets are tables, views, volumes, foreign tables, notebooks and JAR analyses shared into the room. As with shares, the clean room owner must keep enough privilege on each asset indefinitely, and a group owner is advised.
- Notebooks carry reviews in the states APPROVED, PENDING and REJECTED, and a list of collaborators allowed to run them.
- Runs are task runs on serverless compute; results go to an output catalog.
- Deleting a clean room leaves it in the other collaborators' metastores in a deleted state until they delete it too.

Design rules that follow. The exit is the output, so review what the notebook writes: aggregated columns, a minimum group size both parties agree (suppressing groups under 20 is a synthetic example), no identifiers. Approval is the control, so name reviewers on both sides and re-review after any change. Freshness is as of each run; revocation is removing assets or deleting the room, and outputs already written stay with whoever received them.

Where supported: availability by cloud and region, the number of collaborators and billing must be checked on the current Databricks pages before a clean room is proposed. If either party lacks a Unity Catalog metastore the pattern is unavailable, and the choice falls back to what each side may see: an aggregated share, or no collaboration.

beats.recap: A clean room releases only what the approved notebook writes, and needs every collaborator on Unity Catalog.

beats.title: Compare on the same six questions, then decide per direction
beats.outcome: Compare all patterns on six questions and record a conditional decision per direction.
beats.explanation: Put copy, governed share, federation and clean room in one table and answer the same six questions: what moves, who enforces, who pays in kind, how revocation works, how fresh the view is, how it fails. Then decide each direction separately, attach conditions, and rehearse [[dbxfe-sharing-revocation-concept|revocation]] before the first real read. Notice that failures differ in visibility, since a copy fails silently, and that the decision table's rows are conditions, not product names.

handbook.markdown:
The decision record, in the field guide's shape:

1. State who needs what, in which direction, for what decision and for how long.
2. Compare the alternatives on the six questions (the first table in this beat).
3. Mark what each alternative cannot do for this need, including tooling not yet tested.
4. Decide per direction, with conditions: the recipient demonstrates a read on synthetic rows; the shared object excludes identities; an expiry, an IP list and a named contact are set; support for the recipient type is confirmed on the current documentation.
5. Rehearse revocation and record the timings.
6. Write what would change the decision and the fallback for each case.

Worked outcome for Halvern (from the guide, with this module's mechanism added): Cinderline to Halvern, open sharing of one view, conditional on a successful synthetic read from Halvern's notebooks; Halvern to Cinderline, a weekly extract retained like any source file, because Halvern's DBA declined query load and the parameters change weekly.

Failure behaviour differs in visibility, and that matters to operations. A governed share and federation fail loudly (an authorization error, a failed query), so someone notices; a copy fails silently, and a missed export is a gap nobody sees until a number is wrong. Prefer the loud failure where the data drives a decision, and add a freshness check where a copy is unavoidable.

Cost is compared in kind, not money: storage, compute, transfer and people's time per pattern. Real prices need a current source, date, currency, unit and region; without them write "check current pricing".

What would change the choice: the recipient's tooling cannot read the protocol (fall back to an extract with written retention, said plainly to the security lead); a new need where neither side may see rows (examine a clean room); the source's tolerance for load changes (reconsider federation).

beats.recap: Same six questions for every pattern, a decision per direction, and a timed revocation rehearsal.

extensionCards.prompt: How can a recipient read only what changed in a shared table since its last run?
extensionCards.answer: Share the table with its change data feed enabled, so the recipient reads changes between versions instead of re-reading the whole table.
extensionCards.explanation: The protocol's change-data-feed read returns row-level changes between a starting version or timestamp and an optional ending one, adding _change_type (insert, update_preimage, update_postimage, delete), _commit_version and _commit_timestamp. In the Databricks API a shared object carries a cdf_enabled setting, and start_version lets the provider set the lowest version recipients may query. The Python connector exposes it as load_table_changes_as_pandas with starting and ending versions. It suits a supplier's nightly incremental job; the recipient still owns deduplication by version, and a job that falls behind the permitted start version must re-read a full snapshot.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Re-reading a whole shared table every night multiplies transfer; change reads keep a recipient current without repeated full copies.

extensionCards.prompt: How can a non-Databricks recipient read a share without holding a long-lived bearer token?
extensionCards.answer: Use OIDC token federation: the recipient's own identity provider issues short-lived tokens that a federation policy on the recipient validates.
extensionCards.explanation: The Databricks API reference describes recipient federation policies for open sharing: users or applications authenticate with short-lived OIDC tokens from their own identity provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta, and a policy set on the recipient validates the token's claims. It supports a user-to-machine flow, for example a person reading through a BI client, and a machine-to-machine flow for a nightly job. There is no credential file to leak or rotate, and access ends when the grant or policy is removed. It needs the recipient to run an identity-provider integration and both sides to agree which claims are checked.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It removes the commonest open-sharing risk, a copied credential file, for recipients that already run an identity provider.

extensionCards.prompt: How can one share give each supplier only the partitions that belong to it?
extensionCards.answer: Partition the shared table by supplier and let the share's partition filter compare that column with a property of the reading recipient.
extensionCards.explanation: In the Databricks API a shared object's partition value can name a recipient_property_key instead of a fixed value, and every recipient carries key-value properties. Cinderline could set supplier_id to halvern on Halvern's recipient and to orvane on Orvane's, then add one table partitioned by supplier_id whose partition specification refers to that property; in SQL, as previously read, the function is CURRENT_RECIPIENT('supplier_id'). Each recipient then sees only its own partitions from a single object, so adding a supplier means a property and a grant, not a new table. The filter works at partition granularity, so the table's partitioning must match the boundary you need.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It keeps one governed object for many partners instead of a filtered copy per supplier that each needs its own maintenance.

extensionCards.prompt: What changes when a sharing server offers directory-based access instead of per-file URLs?
extensionCards.answer: The server issues temporary cloud credentials for the table's directory, and the client reads the Delta log and files itself until they expire.
extensionCards.explanation: The protocol defines two access modes. With URL-based access the server lists files as pre-signed URLs, each with its own expiry. With directory-based access, the Generate Temporary Table Credential call returns short-lived, read-only credentials (AWS STS keys, an Azure user-delegation SAS or a Google OAuth token) scoped to the table's root, with an expiration time; engines that process the Delta log can then use their own metadata optimizations and caching. Table metadata lists the supported accessModes, and a client that supports only URLs must fail on a directory-only table. Revocation follows the same rule at a coarser grain: credentials already issued work until they expire.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It explains compatibility failures between a recipient's client and a table, and why revocation has an expiry tail in both modes.

recap.title: Three patterns, six questions, one rehearsal
recap.markdown: **A copy moves rows and ends control; a governed share keeps rows in place and checks every read; federation queries the other system where it lives; a clean room shares computation and outputs.** OpenSharing, formerly documented as Delta Sharing, authorizes each request and hands out short-lived file URLs, so revocation stops the next read but not issued URLs or saved copies, and every read is fresh while every saved result goes stale. Pushdown decides federated traffic, and ingestion wins when data is queried often or needs history. UniForm lets Iceberg readers use the same files, sometimes a version late, and the catalog decides who may vend credentials to outside engines. **Transfer challenge:** redo the six-question table for a supplier on Databricks in another region that needs time travel, and name which answers change.

appliedTask.title: One supplier, two needs, two patterns
appliedTask.prompt: Pellmark Polymers, a fictional seal supplier, runs Databricks with Unity Catalog in another cloud region. It wants Cinderline's line 4 rejected-seal inspections each morning, with 30 days of history so it can compare today with any earlier day. Separately, both companies want to correlate Cinderline's warranty returns with Pellmark's compound batches, but neither may see the other's row-level records. Choose a pattern for each need, and for each give the setup, freshness, revocation steps and what remains afterwards, who pays in kind, the failure each side would see, and what you would mark unknown.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Need 1, a Databricks-to-Databricks share. Pellmark sends its sharing identifier and Cinderline creates recipient pellmark_polymers from it, so no token exists. A purpose-built table of line 4 rejected-seal inspections without inspector identity goes into share pellmark_seals, owned by a group that keeps SELECT, with history sharing enabled and a start version set at the version from 30 days before sharing begins, so comparisons reach back a month from day one; the table's own retention settings must keep the files of every version Pellmark may query. Pellmark creates a catalog from the share and grants its analysts. Freshness: the latest version at each read, with time travel inside the window. Cost in kind: Cinderline's storage serves cross-region reads (transfer charges unknown); Pellmark pays its compute. Revocation: revoke SELECT on the share; Pellmark's next query fails; tables Pellmark wrote from it remain under the agreement. Failure: the owner group losing SELECT reads as permission denied; a table feature Pellmark's runtime cannot read fails its queries. Need 2, a clean room, if available in both clouds and regions: each side adds its table, a notebook reviewed by both writes monthly return rates per compound batch above an agreed minimum group size to the output catalog. Freshness: as of each run. Revocation: remove assets or delete the room; outputs already written stay. Unknown: clean room availability and billing, cross-region transfer charges, the legal agreement.
appliedTask.reasoning: Each need is matched to its binding constraint: Pellmark may see the inspection rows and runs Unity Catalog, so a token-free share with history fits; neither side may see the other's warranty or batch rows, so only a clean room fits, conditionally. Every answer follows the six questions and turns availability and billing into verification items.
